title: How HTTPS keeps your data private

narration: Say you log in on shared wifi.
Your password crosses the network to the server.
beats.visual_intent: Browser at left, server at right on the clean field, a row of network nodes between them; a packet reading 'user, password' in plain text travels left to right.

grounding.claim: an illustrative login on shared wifi
on a shared network other devices and the operator may be positioned where they can see traffic on the path

narration: Over plain HTTP,
anyone who can see the path can read it.
beats.visual_intent: A watcher marker sits on one node of the path and copies the packet; the copied text 'password' is plainly readable in the watcher's panel. The watcher is the one loud thing.

grounding.claim: plain HTTP data is readable by anyone who can see traffic on its path

beats.misconception: the network between you and the site is private

narration: HTTPS makes it private in three moves:
prove who, agree a key, scramble.
beats.visual_intent: Three labelled steps appear in order along the bottom as spoken, ready to be lit one at a time through the lesson; the browser and server stay in place above.

grounding.claim: HTTPS provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication

beats.delivery: clear, a beat on each of the three

narration: HTTPS is web traffic wrapped in TLS,
and it opens with a handshake.
beats.visual_intent: The packet is wrapped in a protective outline that reads TLS; browser and server exchange a short hello before the packet moves. Step 1 is lit.

grounding.claim: HTTPS is HTTP carried inside a TLS connection
a handshake runs before any application data is sent

narration: Move one, identity.
The server presents a certificate:
its proof of who it is.
beats.visual_intent: A certificate card with the site's name travels from the server to the browser; the browser lifts it into a checking panel.

grounding.claim: the server presents a digital certificate tying its name to its public key, to prove who it is

narration: The browser checks three things:
a trusted authority issued it,
the name matches the address,
and it has not expired.
beats.visual_intent: On the certificate in the checking panel three rows tick in turn as spoken: issuer traced to a trusted authority, the name beside the typed address, the dates against today. Each tick is the accent while spoken.

grounding.claim: a certificate authority is an organisation browsers already trust
the browser checks issuer, name match and validity dates

narration: Fail any one, and the browser warns you.
beats.visual_intent: One row (the name) turns to a cross and a warning panel stops the packet at the browser; then the three checks all tick again and the first step stays lit.

grounding.claim: if the certificate fails a check the browser shows a warning instead of silently continuing

recall.prompt: Issuer, name, date: three checks before a single byte of the login moves.

narration: Move two, a shared key.
Both ends need the same secret, with the network watching.
beats.visual_intent: Step 2 lights. An empty key slot appears at the browser and at the server; the watcher sits on the path between them, eye open.

grounding.claim: the two sides agree a shared secret session key in the handshake

narration: They run a key exchange.
The key itself never travels
in a form a watcher can use.
beats.visual_intent: Two different coloured signals cross the path in opposite directions; at each end the received signal combines with that side's own, and both slots fill with the identical key. The key is never drawn on the path.

grounding.claim: the key is agreed without ever being sent readable across the network

beats.delivery: slower and plain; let the key land
beats.misconception: the key is simply sent across, perhaps locked, and a watcher could grab it

narration: Even someone who recorded all of it
cannot realistically work the key out.
beats.visual_intent: The watcher's panel holds the two recorded signals and a question mark where the key would be; the two ends hold the matching key. A short held beat.

grounding.claim: an eavesdropper who records every message of the exchange still cannot work out the session key

beats.delivery: slower, plain, with the hedge audible

narration: Move three.
The browser scrambles the login with that key.
Only the two ends can unscramble it.
beats.visual_intent: Step 3 lights. The plain login packet passes through the key at the browser and becomes a block of noise, travels the path, and is turned back into readable text by the same key at the server.

grounding.claim: data is encrypted with the shared session key, the same key at both ends
only the two ends holding the key can turn it back into readable data

narration: The watcher sees only noise,
and any change in transit is detected.
beats.visual_intent: The watcher's panel now fills with unreadable noise. A second packet is altered on the path and the server end rejects it with a clear mark.

grounding.claim: encrypted data looks like meaningless noise to a watcher
if data is altered in transit the receiving end detects the change

narration: Now the padlock:
a private trip to the site named in the address.
beats.visual_intent: A padlock closes beside the address in the browser frame; the address and the verified name sit side by side with the padlock between them.

grounding.claim: the padlock means the connection is private and is with the site named in the address bar

narration: It is not a verdict on the site;
a bad actor can get a certificate for its own name.
It covers the trip,
not what the site does with your data.
on_screen: Not a verdict on the site
beats.visual_intent: The padlock sits on a look-alike address with a mark that it is still only a private trip; the path section between browser and server is highlighted while the server's data store beyond it is outlined as not covered.

grounding.claim: the padlock does not mean the site is honest or safe, because a bad actor can obtain a valid certificate for its own name
HTTPS protects data only while it travels; once it reaches the server the site decides what happens to it

beats.misconception: the padlock means the site is safe and honest

narration: A different site.
A: valid certificate, exact address.
B: trusted issuer, different name.
C: no certificate.
Which gets your password? Pause and decide.
beats.visual_intent: Three option cards on the clean field, each with a small certificate or open-path icon, held still through the pause.

recall.question: Which connection should carry your password?
options: A: a valid certificate for the exact address
B: a certificate from a trusted authority, but for a different name

grounding.claim: an illustrative second site for transfer
the browser checks issuer, name and date

narration: A. All three checks pass.
B fails on name, so the browser warns.
C is readable by anyone.
beats.visual_intent: A is marked right and its three ticks light; B shows the name tick turn to a cross with the browser warning; C shows the plain packet readable to the watcher. Correct is carried by the mark, not only colour.

grounding.claim: the name on the certificate must match the address
a failed check triggers a browser warning
plain HTTP is readable on the path

narration: Back at the login:
the watcher now sees only noise.
Prove who, agree a key, scramble.
That is what the padlock stands for.
beats.visual_intent: The opening scene replayed on the same path: the login packet now travels as noise past the watcher; the three steps light together along the bottom and the padlock settles at the browser. Calm, a held final frame.

grounding.claim: HTTPS provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication
encrypted data looks like noise to a watcher

beats.delivery: level and exact; short and done
